beats.narration_text: This is Onyx, in for Humanitarians AI. Two weeks in, we have a loop that can act. Today, the thing it acts with. Tools. And the part that surprises everyone who builds their first one: the model never sees your code. It sees what you wrote about your code. Which means the documentation is the product.

props.command: What does a model actually receive when I hand it a tool?
output: Three things cross the wire: a name, a description, and a parameter schema.
Your function body is not one of them. It never leaves your machine.
So the description is not documentation about the tool. It is the tool.

beats.act: ACT 1 — WHAT THE MODEL ACTUALLY SEES
beats.narration_text: Everyone writes their first tool the same way. Wire up the function, expose it, done. And then the agent never calls it — or calls it at the worst possible moment. The bug is almost never in the function. It is in the sentence above it.

beats.act: ACT 1 — WHAT THE MODEL ACTUALLY SEES
beats.narration_text: Here is what actually crosses the wire. The name. The description — everything you wrote in the docstring, verbatim. And a parameter schema, derived from your type hints. That is the whole payload. Your function body stays on your machine. The model is choosing from labels, not reading your implementation.

beats.act: ACT 1 — WHAT THE MODEL ACTUALLY SEES
beats.narration_text: And printed out, it looks like this. A name. A description that is just the docstring, word for word. A schema listing the argument and whether it is required. And a last line worth staring at: not sent, the function body. Read only that, and ask whether you could tell when to use it.

beats.act: ACT 2 — THE DESCRIPTION IS THE TOOL
beats.narration_text: This is how that payload gets built. Fourteen lines. The name comes from the function. The description is the docstring, untouched. The parameters come from your type hints, and anything without a default is required. Now notice what is never read anywhere in there. The body.

beats.act: ACT 2 — THE DESCRIPTION IS THE TOOL
beats.narration_text: A description has to answer three questions, and only the first is easy. What comes back. When you should reach for it. And when you should not — which is the one almost nobody writes, and the one that stops an agent grabbing the wrong tool.

beats.act: ACT 2 — THE DESCRIPTION IS THE TOOL
beats.narration_text: Same function. The bodies are byte-identical, and the program checks that for us. Two contracts. One is three words, and answers none of the three questions. The other is two hundred and ninety-two characters, and answers all three. Only the sentence changed. The sentence is what gets read.

beats.narration_text: And every tool you add has a price. It eats context, on every single call. It adds one more thing to be confused with. It widens what a wrong decision can reach. And it becomes a promise you now have to keep working. Four sharp tools beat twenty vague ones.

items: Context — every definition is sent, every call
Ambiguity — one more thing to confuse it with
Blast radius — more that a wrong call can reach
Maintenance — a promise you have to keep working
props.caption: Four sharp tools beat twenty vague ones.

beats.narration_text: So here is the rule. Write the description before you write the function, in the words a caller would actually think in. Name the case where reaching for it is wrong. Then read only the payload — not your code — and ask whether a stranger could choose correctly. If you cannot, neither can the model.

beats.narration_text: So, the verdict. A tool is not a function you expose — it is a contract you write in English, and the model reads the contract, never the code. Three things cross the wire: a name, a description, and a schema derived from your type hints. The description carries almost all of the weight, and it has to say when not to use the tool, not only what it does. And every tool you add costs context, adds ambiguity, and widens the blast radius. A few sharp ones beat a drawer full of vague ones.

props.artifactHeading: A tool is a contract, not a function
artifactLines: A tool is a contract written in English — the model reads the contract, never your code.
Three things cross the wire: the name, the description, and a schema from your type hints.
The description carries the weight, and must say when NOT to use the tool.
Every tool costs context, adds ambiguity, and widens what a wrong call can reach.
Test it by reading only the payload: if a stranger cannot choose, neither can the model.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here is the prompt. Here are two tools I have defined. Read only the names, descriptions and schemas — not my implementations — and tell me which one you would call for each of these five requests, and where you would genuinely be unsure. Then rewrite whichever description caused the confusion. Run that on two of your own tools that do similar things. The unsure list is the whole exercise — that uncertainty is not the model being weak. It is your contract being vague.

The 'unsure' list is the deliverable. It is a map of your vague sentences.
